study.title: Consecutive Acupuncture Stimulations Lead to Significantly Decreased Neural Responses
study.journal: The Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
study.study_design: Within-subject repeated-measures fMRI study; all subjects measured twice in the same scanning session with a block design
study.randomization: Order of physicians performing acupuncture/sham was randomized; participants were not randomized to arm order (acupuncture always preceded sham)
study.blinding: Participants did not know which doctor was performing acupuncture/sham and were told they would get acupuncture stimulations 4 times during fMRI scanning
study.population: Healthy right-handed male volunteers, between 20 and 35 years old (mean age 24.5 ± 3.0 years), who had previously experienced acupuncture treatments
study.inclusion_criteria: Healthy right-handed male volunteers, between 20 and 35 years old, who had previously experienced acupuncture treatments

extraction_notes.note: The paper states coordinates are reported as Talairach coordinates (Table 2 header and text), but the preprocessing used SPM5 with MNI normalization. There is a potential discrepancy between MNI normalization and Talairach coordinate reporting. The paper explicitly labels coordinates as Talairach; no conversion is described.

Table 2 uses 'L' and 'R' to denote hemisphere; the x-coordinate sign is used to infer sign for left hemisphere regions (negative x), but the table reports x values without sign in some rows (e.g., Inferior parietal lobule L: -61 is inferred from the 'L' label and reported 61 in the table). The extracted coordinates are consistent with the L/R labels and the Talairach convention, and negative signs are applied as indicated by the hemisphere column and the table footnote.

The de qi survey instrument is not named. The paper states 'the psychophysical response of every participant was obtained' and 'subjects rated the type and intensity of sensations' but the specific scale or questionnaire used is not described.
No adverse events section is included. The paper does not report on adverse events.
Cluster sizes (voxel counts) for individual peaks/clusters in Tables 2 and 3 are not reported. Only the minimum cluster threshold (>50 voxels) is stated.

The order of acupuncture and sham was fixed (acupuncture always preceded sham) rather than counterbalanced. The paper does not explicitly address this as a limitation regarding order effects for sham.

The sham condition results section states 'During sham, no significant brain activations were found with our threshold (Fig. 3)' — this applies to both sham 1st and sham 2nd conditions. It is ambiguous whether sham 1st and sham 2nd were analyzed separately or together; based on context, it appears they were treated analogously to acupuncture blocks but neither produced significant results.

The paper does not specify whether the statistical analyses for sham conditions were also analyzed as paired-sample t-tests comparing sham 1st vs sham 2nd. Only narrative results ('no significant brain activations were found') are reported for sham.
The flip angle for the BOLD sequence is 90 degrees and for T1 is 10 degrees. The matrix is stated as 64x64 but written in the PDF as '6464' which appears to be an OCR rendering of '64×64'.

The paper reports results of sham 1st and sham 2nd from Figure 3 (brain images) but no coordinate tables for sham conditions. The narrative states no significant activations were found for sham. No coordinates for sham are extractable.

It is unclear whether the 'psychophysical response' survey for de qi was administered after each block separately (i.e., after acup1 and after acup2 separately with each physician attribution) or once after the entire scanning session. The paper states 'After acupuncture, the psychophysical response of every participant was obtained' and Table 1 shows per-physician (P1, P2) ratings, suggesting separate assessments per stimulation.
No expectancy or treatment credibility scales were administered or reported. Blinding check was not formally assessed beyond the narrative description of participant instructions.
